source_span: I would expect our rates strategists to continue leaning towards higher yields absent a major shock, such as a recession or an AI-led equity bust
source_chain: DB's house view is that the current rise in global yields is normalization after the 2010s financial repression, not a fiscal panic, THEREFORE DB's own rates strategists still expect yields to keep climbing from here, THEREFORE because today's higher-yield starting point now carries a much bigger carry cushion than the low-rate 2010s (10Y could reach ~5.5% in a year / ~6.4% in two before total returns turn negative, and a buyer at the Oct-2023 yield peak is already up >16%), holding duration is less painful even as yields keep rising. Invalidation: only a recession or an AI-led equity bust would change DB's continued-higher-yields call.
pulse_chain: Warsh's Jackson Hole pivot flips the market to pricing a September hike as base case, driving a historic global bond selloff (10Y at 4.75%, 'not seen since before the 2008 financial crisis'), THEREFORE this splits into a named bank-vs-bank debate: Deutsche Bank's 'bull case' (normalization, not a crisis; +16% total return since the late-2023 low) versus an unnamed 'structurally higher' camp (deficits, energy, AI capex), THEREFORE the structurally-higher camp wins the next few weeks because a hike is imminent, resolved via Short $TLT, invalidated only if the September FOMC fails to deliver the priced hike or Warsh softens his tone.
why: DB is not the calm, opposing 'bull case' the pulse casts it as — the note explicitly says DB's own rates strategists still expect yields to keep rising from here (the same conclusion the pulse assigns to the opposing camp), and DB's own stated invalidation is a recession or an AI-led equity bust, not a Fed policy outcome, so the pulse both flips DB onto the wrong side of a manufactured debate and swaps in an invalidation DB never argues.
